title: Plan a Lippan panel around relief, spacing and reflected light
description: Learn from a Kachchh craftsperson how a Lippan mud-and-mirror panel uses raised lines and small reflective pieces, and plan a safe, balanced design before shaping clay.
intent: How to approach an artisan-led Lippan panel through motif choice, relief depth, mirror spacing, surface stability and community-specific visual conventions.

sources.title: Handicraft: Kachchh
sources.publisher: District Administration, Kachchh, Government of Gujarat
sources.purpose: Describes Lippan Kaam as a Kachchh mud-and-mirror mural practice and notes variation in community visual conventions.

sections.heading: Ask who made the example and where it belongs
paragraphs: Lippan Kaam is a Kachchh mud-and-mirror mural practice, not a generic clay craft. The district administration describes it as a traditional mural form and notes that different communities in Kachchh have distinct styles. Before drawing, ask the craftsperson how they name their own work, what the sample represents, and which motifs they are comfortable teaching in a short session.

A workshop panel is a chance to study decisions, not to claim authority over the tradition. Ask whether the design is a geometric study, a small adaptation of a household pattern, or a motif with a context you should understand. If the artist says a form is not appropriate to copy, take that as part of the lesson.

sections.heading: Sketch relief before placing mirrors
paragraphs: Draw the panel as raised paths and open spaces before the clay is added. A repeated diamond, circle or radiating line can help you plan how raised borders will meet, but choose a simple composition that fits the size of the base. Mark where each mirror will sit so that you can see whether the open spaces remain balanced.

Ask how much relief your workshop material can hold without slumping or cracking. Different clay mixtures and bases behave differently, so let the artisan set the depth and method. The point of the sketch is to make placement visible, not to impose a standard pattern on every artisan’s version of Lippan.

sections.heading: Shape the clay lines with an even hand
paragraphs: Observe the craftsperson preparing the clay and attaching the raised lines to the surface. Ask how they judge consistency: perhaps by how the line compresses, how the join closes, or whether the relief stays attached when the panel is tilted. Start with a short border, then add a curve or turn that shows whether your pressure changes around corners.

Avoid trying to repair a weak join by adding more material everywhere. If the line lifts, ask the artisan whether the surface needs preparation or the clay needs a different amount of moisture. Keep the panel supported and follow their drying instructions. Fine cracks, loose edges and uneven height are useful signals to diagnose before the mirror pieces are set.

sections.heading: Set mirrors with the maker’s safety method
paragraphs: Small mirrors catch light and make a raised pattern change as the viewer moves, but broken or sharp-edged pieces need careful handling. Let the artisan select the pieces and show how they are set into the clay. Do not cut mirror, use an unknown adhesive, or handle broken shards on your own. Ask whether safe-edged pieces are part of this session and how to hold the panel while setting them.

Place each mirror only where the design and clay support it. A row of evenly spaced reflective shapes can establish a rhythm, while a single misplaced one may interrupt the pattern. Stand the panel at several angles if the instructor allows, and notice where reflections draw the eye. That gives you a practical way to evaluate the layout before the clay dries.

sections.heading: Read the finished surface in changing light
paragraphs: After the panel dries according to the artisan’s process, look at it from straight on and from the side. The relief should create shadows as well as reflections; the mirrors are not merely decoration on a flat board. Ask the craftsperson which parts of the pattern read most clearly and whether the panel would be used indoors or as a wall surface in their own practice.

Write down the community and the terms the artist used, along with the material and one design decision you learned. Kachchh’s district description notes that visual conventions can differ across communities, so avoid presenting your panel as the Lippan style. A thoughtful next step is to learn about the maker’s own pattern vocabulary or see another practitioner’s interpretation with permission.
